en: Did you read my email?
context: Checking if a colleague saw your mail.
explain: 'Did' starts a past question, and the main verb stays in the base form.
usage: Use it politely with a teammate who has not responded to your mail.
leelaQ: How often do you check your emails?
answer: I check them in the morning, after lunch and in the evening.

en: Kindly review the document and share your comments.
context: Asking a colleague to check a document.
explain: Two actions joined with 'and'. 'Review' means to check carefully.
usage: Use it in an email when you want someone to check your document.
leelaQ: What do you do before you send a document?
answer: I read it twice and ask a friend to check it.

en: I am sharing my screen now.
tamil: நான் இப்போ என் ஸ்கிரீனை ஷேர் பண்றேன்.
context: Starting a screen share in an online meeting.
explain: 'Am sharing' tells what you are doing at this moment.
usage: Use it in an online meeting before you show a presentation or file.
leelaQ: Do you attend online meetings?
answer: Yes, I attend two or three online meetings every week.

en: How is the work going?
context: Checking on a colleague's progress in a friendly way.
explain: 'How is ... going' is a casual way to ask for an update.
usage: Use it as a friendly check-in with a teammate or junior.
leelaQ: How is your work going these days?
answer: It is going well, but I am a bit busy.

en: I can take this task if nobody is free.
tamil: யாரும் ஃப்ரீயா இல்லன்னா இந்த வேலையை நான் எடுத்துக்குறேன்.
context: Offering to help the team with extra work.
explain: 'Can' shows that you are ready and able. 'If' gives the condition.
usage: Use it when your team is short of people and you want to help.
leelaQ: When do you offer to help your teammates?
answer: I offer help when they have too much work.

en: Can we move the review to Thursday afternoon?
context: Asking to change the time of a review.
explain: 'Can we move' is a friendly way to ask for a new time.
usage: Use it when you have another urgent task on the planned day.
leelaQ: What do you do if you cannot attend a review on time?
answer: I tell my manager early and ask for another time.

en: What is your opinion on this plan?
tamil: இந்த பிளானைப் பத்தி உங்க கருத்து என்ன?
context: Asking a teammate to share a view in a discussion.
explain: 'Opinion' means what you personally think about something.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you want everyone to share their views.
leelaQ: Do you like to share your ideas in team meetings?
answer: Yes, I share my ideas, but I listen to others first.

en: I have worked with this client for two years.
tamil: நான் இந்த கிளையன்ட்டோட ரெண்டு வருஷமா வேலை பண்றேன்.
context: Saying how long you know the client.
explain: 'For two years' with 'have worked' means it started in the past and is still going.
usage: Use it in an interview or meeting to show your experience.
leelaQ: How long have you worked in your company?
answer: I have worked here for three years.

en: Please find the details in the attached file.
context: Writing a formal email with an attachment.
explain: 'Please find' is a common formal phrase in business emails.
usage: Use it in a formal email when you send details as an attachment.
leelaQ: How do you start an email with details?
answer: I write a short greeting and then I mention the attached file.

en: I respectfully disagree with that point.
context: Disagreeing politely with a senior in a meeting.
explain: 'Respectfully' makes a disagreement sound polite and professional.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you do not accept someone's idea but want to be polite.
leelaQ: How do you disagree with someone at work?
answer: I stay calm and say I respectfully disagree, and then I give my reason.

en: We have a team lunch on Friday.
context: Inviting a new colleague to join the group.
explain: The simple present can talk about fixed future events like a plan.
usage: Use it to inform or invite a colleague about a group event.
leelaQ: Does your team go out for lunch together?
answer: Yes, we go out once a month to a nearby restaurant.

en: I have already informed the whole team.
context: Telling your manager the team knows about the change.
explain: 'Have informed' with 'already' shows the work is done before now.
usage: Use it when your manager asks if everyone knows about an announcement.
leelaQ: How do you tell your team about a change?
answer: I send a short message to the group and also tell them in person.

en: I will join the call in five minutes.
context: Messaging the team when you are a little late.
explain: 'In five minutes' means five minutes from now.
usage: Use it in a chat when you are not able to join an online call on time.
leelaQ: What do you say if you are late for a call?
answer: I say I will join in a few minutes and say sorry.

en: Did we miss anything important?
context: Checking at the end of a meeting.
explain: A good closing question. It shows that you care about the details.
usage: Use it at the end of a meeting or when you check a list before sending.
leelaQ: What do you check before you end a meeting?
answer: I check the action points and who will do them.

en: Are you facing any problem with this task?
tamil: இந்த வேலையில உங்களுக்கு ஏதாவது பிரச்சனை இருக்கா?
context: Asking a junior colleague if they need help.
explain: 'Facing a problem' is a common phrase in Indian English for 'having a problem'.
usage: Use it as a senior when a teammate looks stuck.
leelaQ: What problem did you face at work recently?
answer: I could not find a file, and my colleague helped me.

en: Who will write the minutes of this meeting?
context: Asking at the start of a team meeting.
explain: 'Minutes' are the written record of a meeting.
usage: Use it at the start of a meeting so that someone takes the responsibility.
leelaQ: Do you ever write the minutes for your team?
answer: Yes, I write them sometimes when my turn comes.

en: Don't blame anyone, just fix the issue.
tamil: யாரையும் குத்தம் சொல்லாதீங்க, பிரச்சனையை சரி பண்ணுங்க.
context: Calming a team during a work problem.
explain: 'Don't' plus a verb is a negative order. The second part gives the right action.
usage: Use it as a team lead when people are arguing about whose mistake it was.
leelaQ: Why is it better to solve a problem than blame someone?
answer: Because blaming wastes time and the problem remains.

en: Will you be at the team meeting tomorrow?
context: Checking a colleague's presence.
explain: 'Will you be at' asks about presence at a future event.
usage: Use it when you plan a discussion and need someone to attend.
leelaQ: Will you attend any meeting tomorrow?
answer: Yes, I have a review meeting at eleven.

en: Where did you save the final file?
context: Looking for a document in a shared folder.
explain: 'Where did you' asks about a place in the past. 'Save' stays in the base form.
usage: Use it when a teammate shares a file and you cannot find it.
leelaQ: Where do you keep your office files?
answer: I keep them in a shared folder and also on my laptop.

en: Can you help me with this report?
context: Asking a senior colleague for help.
explain: 'Help me with' is followed by the task.
usage: Use it with a senior colleague when you are stuck on your work.
leelaQ: Who do you ask for help at work?
answer: I ask my senior colleague because he is kind and knows a lot.

en: I will send the report by tomorrow evening.
context: Promising a manager when the report will come.
explain: 'Will' makes a promise. 'By' gives the last time for the work.
usage: Use it with a manager or client when you promise a time for your work.
leelaQ: When will you send your next report?
answer: I will send my next report by Friday afternoon.

en: She is preparing the presentation for the review.
tamil: அவங்க ரிவியூக்கான பிரசன்டேஷனை தயார் பண்ணிட்டு இருக்காங்க.
context: Explaining where a colleague is right now.
explain: 'Is preparing' shows work in progress.
usage: Use it when someone asks about a colleague who is busy with a task.
leelaQ: Have you made a presentation at work?
answer: Yes, I made one last month for our project review.

en: He never comes late to meetings.
tamil: அவர் மீட்டிங்குக்கு ஒருநாளும் லேட்டா வர மாட்டாரு.
context: Praising a punctual colleague.
explain: 'Never' already makes the sentence negative, so do not add 'not'.
usage: Use it to talk about a colleague who is always on time.
leelaQ: Who is always on time in your office?
answer: My team lead is always on time for every meeting.

en: How long will the meeting take?
context: Asking the organiser about the time you need to keep free.
explain: 'How long' asks about the amount of time.
usage: Use it before a meeting when you need to plan your other work.
leelaQ: How long are your meetings usually?
answer: Most of them are thirty minutes to one hour.

en: Do you have five minutes to talk?
context: Asking a colleague for a short chat.
explain: Mentioning the time tells the person the talk will be short.
usage: Use it before you speak to a busy teammate so you do not disturb them.
leelaQ: How do you talk to a busy colleague?
answer: I ask politely if they have a few minutes first.
